bull_bear.body: Equity infusion by Hella: ₹345 crore (February 2022); ₹150 crore (2023)
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body: Intense competition, volatility in raw material prices, high debt levels
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Parent company Hella's support and guidance may help Shalimar Paints Limited navigate challenges
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- 125-year heritage brand (established 1902) with a legacy of protecting Indian landmarks (Howrah Bridge, Rashtrapati Bhavan, Chenab River rail bridge)
- Awarded 'Most Trusted Brand' in the Indian paints sector two years in a row
- Nationwide distribution network of 47 sales depots and 7,500+ retail touchpoints, complemented by a growing dedicated distributor model for rural/semi-urban penetration
- State-of-the-art R&D centre at Nashik driving low-VOC, lead-free and premiumised product innovation
- Rising share of water-based (low-VOC) paints (~64% of decorative sales) supporting higher gross margins
- Established position as a leading coating supplier in the organised metal-packaging (can coatings) segment in India
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw-material supply-chain dependency — The paint industry, including the Company, is highly dependent on a complex global supply chain for crude-oil-derivative, pigment, resin, solvent, additive and packaging inputs, a significant portion of which are imported or linked to global commodity markets; geopolitical conflicts, trade restrictions, shipping delays, port congestion and freight-cost fluctuations can disrupt availability and inflate input costs.
- Foreign-currency exposure — Exposure to foreign currency transactions for raw-material imports subjects the Company to risk from currency volatility.
- Climate / monsoon risk — Increasing frequency of climate-related events, such as a prolonged monsoon, may disrupt operations in certain geographies, impact raw-material availability, or necessitate changes in manufacturing processes; an extended monsoon was cited as a demand headwind in FY26.
- Negative credit-rating outlook — The Company's long-term bank facilities rating was reaffirmed at 'CARE BB+; Negative' (short-term 'CARE A4+') by CARE Ratings, signalling continuing financial stress and a negative outlook on debt-servicing capacity.
- Government/public-sector funding dependency in Industrial Coatings — The Industrial Paints segment's demand from Iron & Steel and infrastructure customers was disrupted when Central government funds into the Jal Jeevan Mission were halted pending a CAG audit, and by election-year delays in fund releases to contractors across West Bengal, Karnataka and other states, leading to lengthy credit/collection cycles.
- Sustained operating losses / no dividend capacity — The Company reported losses during the year under review, and consequently the Board did not recommend any dividend for FY 2025-26, reflecting ongoing pressure on profitability and reinvestment capacity.
- Cybersecurity and data-protection threat landscape — Management flagged an increasingly complex cybersecurity threat landscape and is only in the process of aligning data governance/privacy practices with the emerging Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) framework, indicating an evolving compliance and security exposure.

business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body: Shalimar Paints Limited develops, manufactures, markets and distributes a comprehensive range of decorative paints and industrial coatings for residential, commercial, institutional and industrial customers. The Decorative Paints division (~63-67% of revenue) covers interior/exterior emulsions, enamels, waterproofing and ancillary tinting/painting products sold through a nationwide dealer and distributor network, while the Industrial Coatings division serves protective-coatings customers in the Steel, Minerals, Metals & Mining sectors and supplies specialised coatings for metal packaging (cans, caps) and pipelines.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Decorative Paints:** Hero (Weather Guard 12, Insignia), Zero Damp (waterproofing), Magic (ancillary tools/accessories), Mela (rural undercoat/topcoat), Superlac Enamel (PU enamel), Color Space (tinting system)
- **Industrial Coatings:** TUFFKOTE (protective coatings for plant & machinery, infrastructure), Can Coatings (Size, Base, Varnish, lacquer for tin cans, beverage/food cans, caps), Pipeline coatings (cathodic protection, corrosion resistance)

outlook.body: Outlook: Negative; Strategy: Focus on cost optimization, improving operational efficiency, and expanding product portfolio
outlook.title: Guidance / outlook

outlook.body: Expansion into new markets, increasing market share in existing segments
outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- "Shalimar 2.0" transformation to reimagine manufacturing, product innovation, customer engagement and digital capabilities and rebuild the Company into a modern, agile, technology-driven organisation, guided by a vision of becoming one of India's top-five paint companies
- Modernization programme across the Sikandrabad, Nashik and Chennai manufacturing facilities (capacity augmentation, automation, productivity enhancement) alongside upgrade of the Nashik R&D Centre
- Innovation-led premiumization strategy: continued new-product launches across emulsion, enamel and waterproofing categories (Hero, Superlac, Zero Damp, Magic, Mela brands) spanning premium to value price points
- Accelerated distributor-led business model to deepen penetration in rural and semi-urban markets and Tier2/Tier3 cities, with last-mile delivery focus
- Cost optimization initiatives to offset input-cost inflation: sourcing via reverse auctions, increased direct imports of select raw materials, and R&D-led formulation optimization
- Industrial Coatings segment strategic shift away from the traditional pipeline-coating business model toward core protective coatings, with sales organization re-focused on zonal opportunities
- Brand-equity building through ATL marketing, Bollywood film collaborations/celebrity campaigns, and the Shalimar Expert Painter Loyalty Program to strengthen trust and consumer engagement
- Digital transformation of procurement, sales and business processes through greater automation and digitalization
- The Company's stated capital-risk-management policy is to maintain an adequate capital base to sustain creditor and market confidence and support future development, using appropriate means to enhance or reduce capital as needed. It maintains a Board-approved Dividend Distribution Policy formulated under Regulation 43A of the SEBI Listing Regulations (available on the Company's website); no specific payout ratio or quantum is stated in the text provided.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The Company is pursuing an ongoing modernization programme across its three operating manufacturing facilities — Sikandrabad, Nashik and Chennai — covering capacity augmentation, automation and productivity enhancement, alongside an upgrade of the Research & Development Centre at Nashik (which became fully operational in FY25). During FY 2025-26 all three plants underwent further automation focused on waste reduction, throughput enhancement and quality control. On the distribution side, the Company installed over 250 tinting machines during the year to support incremental emulsion sales, and launched/expanded a dedicated distributor-led model to deepen coverage in rural and remote regions.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Indian paint industry estimated to grow ~12% over the next 4-5 years, with industry turnover estimated to reach Rs 120,000 crore by 2030
- Low per-capita paint consumption in India (~4-5 kg) versus global average (~13-15 kg) indicates substantial headroom for growth and premiumization
- Repainting cycle has shortened from ~5 years to ~3 years, structurally increasing paint consumption frequency
- Premiumization theme: rising consumer preference for high-performance, low-VOC, water-based and multifunctional coatings, plus growing demand for waterproofing solutions
- Organized sector continuing to consolidate share, now commanding over 80% of the market, with established brands expanding into Tier2/Tier3 cities
- FY 2025-26 industry growth was almost flat due to extended monsoon, muted urban demand, delayed discretionary spending and geopolitical uncertainty, with gradual recovery in H2 aided by festive consumption and price increases
- Steep input-cost inflation across the industry was largely deferred and passed through via a sharp price increase in Q4 FY26
- Decorative Paints remained the primary growth engine (~63-67% of total revenue) while Industrial Coatings declined due to an Iron & Steel sector production slowdown, a halt in Jal Jeevan Mission government funding pending a CAG audit, and election-year delays in contractor fund releases across West Bengal, Karnataka and other states
- Q4 FY26 raw-material price volatility linked to the Gulf War raised input costs; only a portion of the impact was passed on to customers in March, with the full impact expected to flow through in subsequent quarters
- Rising water-based paint mix (64% of decorative sales) is improving gross margins given the higher profitability profile of water-based formulations
- Industrial Coatings segment continues to hold accounts across the Steel, Minerals, Metals and Mining sector with Jindal Steel & Power, Jindal Steel Limited, Lloyds Metals & Energy, Shyam Metalics Group, MSPL (Baldota Group), NMDC and Rungta Mines and Minerals, and added new accounts with ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel, Star Metal and Kalyani Ispat
- Consolidated presence in the Karnataka Irrigation and Drinking Water sector through contractors including Shankaranarayana Constructions, Sree UGCL Projects, Sri Srinivasa Constructions, Suprada Constructions and Amrutha Constructions
- Truck body and Agriculture & Construction equipment segment foray has painted close to 10,000 assemblies since entry a year back
